problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary  

**a. Verdict** – I have obtained a complete solution.  
The smallest possible number of rectangular tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Structure of the uncovered squares** –  
   Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit
   square, the uncovered squares form a *permutation matrix*: there is a
   bijection \(\pi:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that the uncovered
   cell in row \(i\) is \((i,\pi(i))\).  All other cells must be covered.

2. **A universal lower bound \(2n-2\)** –  
   *Classification of tiles.*  
   For a tile \(T\) let  

   \[
   L(T)=\min\{j\mid (i,j)\in T\},\qquad
   R(T)=\max\{j\mid (i,j)\in T\}.
   \]

   If a row \(i\) meets \(T\) then the hole \((i,\pi(i))\) cannot lie inside
   \(T\); consequently either \(\pi(i)>R(T)\) (the hole is strictly to the
   right of the whole tile) or \(\pi(i)<L(T)\) (the hole is strictly to the
   left).  Hence every tile is of **left type** (all its rows have holes to
   the right) or **right type** (all its rows have holes to the left).

   *Left‑type tiles.*  
   Consider a left‑type tile \(T\).  Its rightmost column \(R(T)\) is the same
   for all rows covered by \(T\).  If two distinct left‑type tiles had the
   same value of \(R\), their row intervals could be merged into a single
   larger rectangle (still left‑type), contradicting maximality of a tiling.
   Therefore distinct left‑type tiles have distinct values of \(R\).

   For each column \(c\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) the cells of that column that lie
   **below** the hole in column \(c\) (i.e. the cells \((i,c)\) with
   \(\pi(i)>c\)) must be covered, and they can be covered only by a left‑type
   tile whose rightmost column is exactly \(c\) (a right‑type tile never
   reaches column \(c\)).  Hence there must be at least one left‑type tile
   for every \(c=1,\dots ,n-1\); consequently  

   \[
   \#\text{left‑type tiles}\ge n-1 .
   \]

   *Right‑type tiles.*  
   By symmetry the same argument applied to rows gives at least one
   right‑type tile for each row index \(r=1,\dots ,n-1\).  Thus  

   \[
   \#\text{right‑type tiles}\ge n-1 .
   \]

   Adding the two sides yields the universal lower bound  

   \[
   \boxed{\text{any admissible tiling uses at least }2n-2\text{ tiles}.}
   \]

3. **Construction attaining the bound** –  
   Choose the permutation \(\pi(i)=i\); the uncovered squares are the
   diagonal cells \((i,i)\), \(i=1,\dots ,n\).

   *Vertical (left) tiles.*  
   For each \(k=1,2,\dots ,n-1\) place the rectangle  

   \[
   V_{k}= \{(i,k)\mid i=k+1,k+2,\dots ,n\},
   \]

   a \((n-k)\times 1\) tile occupying column \(k\) and all rows below the
   diagonal cell of that column.

   *Horizontal (right) tiles.*  
   For each \(k=1,2,\dots ,n-1\) place the rectangle  

   \[
   H_{k}= \{(k,j)\mid j=k+1,k+2,\dots ,n\},
   \]

   a \(1\times (n-k)\) tile occupying row \(k\) and all columns to the right
   of the diagonal cell of that row.

   The family  

   \[
   \mathcal T=\{V_{1},\dots ,V_{n-1},\,H_{1},\dots ,H_{n-1}\}
   \]

   consists of exactly \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) rectangles.  
   *Disjointness*: each \(V_{k}\) lies entirely in column \(k\) while each
   \(H_{k}\) lies entirely in row \(k\); the only possible intersection would
   be the cell \((k,k)\), which is the uncovered diagonal cell, so the
   rectangles are pairwise disjoint.  
   *Coverage*: every non‑diagonal cell \((i,j)\) with \(i\neq j\) satisfies
   either \(j<i\) (it lies below the diagonal) and is therefore in the
   vertical tile \(V_{j}\), or \(j>i\) (it lies above the diagonal) and is in
   the horizontal tile \(H_{i}\).  Hence all non‑diagonal cells are covered,
   and each row and each column contains exactly one uncovered cell—the
   diagonal one.

   Thus the lower bound \(2n-2\) is attainable.

4. **Application to the original board** –  
   For the given \(2025\times2025\) grid we have \(n=2025\).  Substituting in
   the formula gives  

   \[
   \text{minimum number of tiles}=2\cdot2025-2=4048 .
   \]

   The explicit tiling described above (vertical tiles below the main diagonal
   and horizontal tiles to the right of the diagonal) uses exactly 4048
   tiles and satisfies all the required conditions.

\[
\boxed{4048}
\]
